transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-06-30
Time: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 38 mins
Attendees: Jared Kim (Redwood AE); Priya Shah (Redwood SE); Maya Ortiz (Skyline CTO); Liam Chen (Head of ML); Nadia Park (Platform Eng); Ethan Ruiz (SRE); Olivia Park (Product)

Summary: Quick intro, current infra and SLOs, then deep dive on latency/throughput, followed by bench/next steps recap.

[00:00] Jared Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intros - I'm Jared on AE, Priya's our SE who will run the technical bit.
[00:12] Maya Ortiz: Hi all, Maya here. We're trying to replace a mix of in-house endpoints and a cloud provider for our payment auth conversational flows. Main ask is very tight p95 latency.
[00:24] Liam Chen: Liam - we also have merchant support chat with streaming responses; want to understand token/sec and concurrency.
[00:36] Priya Shah: Great, can you share your current p95 and concurrency targets? That'll drive whether Hosted, Dedicated, or Private makes sense.
[00:48] Nadia Park: We're targeting p95 < 250ms for short auth prompts (like 30-80 tokens) and p95 < 600ms for longer chat agent responses (200-600 tokens). Burst concurrency up to 2000 QPS for auth flows but really short tail; sustained concurrency more like 200-300.
[01:20] Ethan Ruiz: For the auth flow we do synchronous calls in our critical path so anything above 300ms p95 starts to affect conversion.
[01:32] Priya Shah: OK that's helpful. Two things to confirm: token length distribution, and whether streaming is required (i.e., do you need first-byte streaming vs full response).
[01:44] Olivia Park: For merchant support chat we prefer streaming - users see tokens as they arrive - but auth is non-streaming, needs whole response.
[01:56] Jared Kim: From Redwood's perspective, for short prompts with strict p95 we typically recommend Dedicated if isolation and predictable SLOs are needed, but Hosted with pinned model variants + routing can hit tight p95 too depending on load shape.
[02:12] Priya Shah: And there are knobs: quantization/model size, batching windows, KV caching for prefixes, and routing policies. We'll propose a benchmark that tests p95 at target token lengths and concurrency.
[02:28] Liam Chen: Can you explain how batching affects p95? We're worried stacking requests for cost savings increases tail latency.
[02:36] Priya Shah: Sure. Continuous batching helps throughput and cost - for high token/sec workloads it amortizes kernel overhead. But we have adaptive batching and deadline-aware batching: for low-latency paths we use very short batching windows to prioritize p95, and you can configure per-route latency SLOs.
[02:56] Maya Ortiz: What's the typical token/sec throughput / GPU we can expect for say a 7B-like open model?
[03:04] Priya Shah: Very approximate - on an A100 style equivalently provisioned node, you might see 200-1000 tokens/sec per GPU for generation workloads depending on sequence length and quantization. But for small prompts, latency dominates more than raw tokens/sec.
[03:24] Ethan Ruiz: For auth we send about 120 chars average, so ~25 tokens. So p95 being under 250ms is the crux.
[03:34] Priya Shah: For 25-token prompts, with proper prefix caching and minimal batching we can get single-digit tens of ms compute time, but end-to-end includes network, routing, and decoding. We'll include network delta in our benchmarks.
[03:50] Jared Kim: Also important - consistent KV cache for repeated prefixes (we saw you mentioned template-based auth prompts) can reduce compute significantly.
[04:02] Nadia Park: Yes, templates for auth are common. We'll provide representative prompts.
[04:10] Priya Shah: About streaming: streaming introduces small first-byte latency overhead in some runtime paths, but helps perceived latency for chat. Streaming and non-streaming endpoints can be configured separately.
[04:24] Liam Chen: For benchmark methodology, can you run token/sec saturation tests and also p95 at our concurrency profile?
[04:32] Priya Shah: Absolutely - we'll do two types: 1) p95 latency bench at target token sizes and concurrency pattern (auth: bursts, chat: sustained), and 2) token/sec saturation to characterize GPU tokens/sec and points where latency jumps.
[04:48] Maya Ortiz: Are there documented thresholds where you see p95 spikes? Like at certain batch sizes or queue depth?
[04:56] Priya Shah: Yes - when queue depth increases, batching windows get longer; if you have many small concurrent requests they can be batched into larger micro-batches causing tail increases. Our runtime uses deadline-aware dispatch to avoid long waits for latency-sensitive routes. We'll include per-route queue/latency histograms.
[05:18] Ethan Ruiz: Security questions - if we go Dedicated or Private, is key management supported? We need KMS/HSM integration and audit logs.
[05:26] Jared Kim: Yes, Dedicated supports KMS integrations and audit logs; Private offers customer-managed KMS and full on-prem options. We'll attach our security pack.
[05:34] Olivia Park: Cost is also a major factor. Dedicated has higher baseline cost but predictable. Hosted is cheaper for low sustained usage. Curious how to model cost for our blended pattern (bursty auth + sustained chat).
[05:48] Priya Shah: We'll provide a cost projection in the pricing sheet - typical pattern: Hosted + autoscale for bursts is cheaper if you can tolerate some variability; Dedicated gives tight p95 SLAs for critical paths. Also routing by policy lets you route auth to Dedicated and less-critical chat to Hosted.
[06:06] Maya Ortiz: Can Redwood do hybrid routing automatically? We want failover to Hosted if Dedicated capacity is saturated.
[06:12] Jared Kim: Yes, smart routing with fallback to compatible model variants is supported - you can define priority, latency vs cost tiers, and automatic fallback.
[06:20] Liam Chen: Back to benchmarking specifics: we need p95 <250ms for 25-token prompts at up to 2000 QPS peak bursts, and p95 <600ms for 200-600 token responses at 200-300 concurrency. Can you realistically show that?
[06:36] Priya Shah: The 2000 QPS burst is the challenging piece - if those are extremely short-lived (seconds), Hosted with autoscaling + cold start optimizations might handle it, but Dedicated with warm pools and pinned capacity gives the most predictable p95. For 200-300 sustained concurrency on long responses, Dedicated or high provisioned Hosted capacity with batching is required. We'll design the bench to replicate your burst profile (ramp and hold) and include a mixed workload run.
[06:58] Maya Ortiz: We also need streaming latency for chat: first-byte p50 ideally < 150ms, p95 < 350ms.
[07:06] Priya Shah: We'll measure first-byte and end-to-end. Streaming usually has slightly higher first-byte due to framing, but we tune for it.
[07:18] Ethan Ruiz: Do you support client-side retry/backoff patterns we should use to avoid thundering herds?
[07:24] Priya Shah: Yes - we recommend jittered exponential backoff and recommend queueing on the client for non-critical flows. For critical auth we avoid retries; instead rely on capacity and SLOs.
[07:36] Olivia Park: Can you quantify overheads for conversion from float model to int8 quantized variants? Any p95 tradeoffs?
[07:44] Priya Shah: Quantization reduces memory and increases throughput, usually improving latency for generation, but accuracy tradeoffs exist. We'll include a model/quantization recommendation outlining token/sec and p95 differences.
[07:58] Liam Chen: For the bench we'd like both a baseline open model (7B-ish) and a heavier 13B variant to see sensitivity.
[08:06] Priya Shah: Noted. We'll run 7B quantized and 13B q4 variants. We'll report tokens/sec per GPU, p50/p95 latency, and cost per 1M tokens.
[08:18] Maya Ortiz: How do you measure and report network overheads - our users are global and latency varies by region.
[08:24] Priya Shah: We'll run clients from representative geos or simulate added RTTs. For Hosted we can pick regions; Dedicated can be in your VPC region. We'll include network RTT in end-to-end metrics.
[08:40] Jared Kim: Quick note - for the auth path, consider edge prefiltering so you only call the model for ambiguous cases which reduces peak. That often helps economics.
[08:50] Olivia Park: We can do that.
[08:54] Maya Ortiz: Any compliance blockers for payments? We need PCI considerations and auditability.
[08:58] Jared Kim: Redwood doesn't handle cardholder data unless you send it - we recommend tokenization. Dedicated/Private helps with compliance posture and audit logs; we'll share our security pack.
[09:10] Liam Chen: On the bench outputs, we want the raw traces so we can run our own analysis. Will you provide logs and histograms?
[09:16] Priya Shah: Yes - we'll provide raw latency traces, per-token timing, batching windows, queue depth, and GPU utilization metrics.
[09:26] Ethan Ruiz: For the 2000 QPS bursts, can you simulate ingress patterns - e.g., sudden ramp vs 5-second ramp? It matters.
[09:34] Priya Shah: We'll vary ramps - instantaneous spike, 5s, and 30s ramps - and capture p95 and error rates.
[09:40] Olivia Park: If Dedicated is needed, how long to provision a warm pool? We need to know lead time for capacity planning.
[09:46] Jared Kim: Lead time depends on contracted capacity; initial warm provisioning for a Dedicated pool can take 1-2 weeks for reserved capacity, but we support burst capacity and short-term add-ons. We'll detail timelines in the pricing doc.
[10:00] Maya Ortiz: Can you give a rough cost-per-1M token for Hosted vs Dedicated? Ballpark is OK.
[10:06] Priya Shah: Ballpark - Hosted might be 0.8-1.5x per-token cost of Dedicated when you're highly utilized; Dedicated amortizes fixed infra so at scale it's cheaper per token. We'll send a customized cost model for your traffic.
[10:18] Liam Chen: For our team, the SE will need to run an end-to-end POC with our SREs. What instrumentation do you require from our side?
[10:26] Priya Shah: We need representative prompts, concurrency pattern, network locations, and an SRE contact for load injection and monitoring. We'll coordinate on test harness (we provide a JMeter/locust-like runner).
[10:38] Olivia Park: Let's talk about error handling - at what saturation point do you return 429s vs queue?
[10:44] Priya Shah: We have configurable queueing policies and rejection thresholds. For critical SLO routes you can reserve concurrency; beyond that you get configurable 429 behavior. We'll show the controls in the console demo.
[10:56] Maya Ortiz: For the streaming chat p95 targets, if we serve partial tokens, the perceived responsiveness is different. How will you present first-byte vs full-response metrics?
[11:04] Priya Shah: We'll separate first-byte, chunk intervals, and end-to-end completion times, and show cumulative distribution.
[11:14] Liam Chen: Can Redwood run bench on our private deployment if we want to go Private?
[11:20] Jared Kim: For Private/on-prem we can run bench with our SE onsite or via remote access; setup lead time is longer. Typically bench with Private happens post-installation, but we can do a simulated lab run against similar hardware.
[11:34] Ethan Ruiz: Any limitations on concurrent streaming connections per session? We have lots of mobile clients.
[11:40] Priya Shah: Not hard limits - we scale load balancers and streaming proxies; you'll need to size connection counts in Dedicated/Private. We'll measure connection overhead in the bench.
[11:50] Olivia Park: Ok this is good. Can we get an example bench plan and checklist?
[11:54] Jared Kim: Yes - we'll attach a bench plan with scenarios: auth burst (25 tokens, 2k QPS spike), chat sustained (200-600 tokens, 200-300 concurrency), mixed workload, streaming checks, and saturation runs.
[12:08] Maya Ortiz: On the streaming stack - do you use gRPC streams or HTTP chunking? We need compatibility with existing mobile libraries.
[12:16] Priya Shah: We support HTTP/2 streaming and gRPC depending on deployment. We'll confirm client SDK compatibility.
[12:24] Liam Chen: For token/sec per GPU, you mentioned ranges. Will your bench report tokens/sec normalized by token length?
[12:30] Priya Shah: Yes - tokens/sec per GPU and tokens/sec per dollar, across sequence lengths.
[12:36] Ethan Ruiz: If we get p95 regressions post-rollout, how do rollbacks work?
[12:40] Jared Kim: We support rollouts with canary and automatic rollback policies tied to quality/regression metrics. We'll show the rollout controls in the Console demo.
[12:52] Olivia Park: Great. Let's talk timeline: we want bench results within two weeks. Is that feasible?
[12:58] Jared Kim: If you provide prompts and traffic profile by July 2, we can run initial Hosted/Dedicated lab benches and share results by July 9-10. Private will take longer.
[13:10] Maya Ortiz: Sounds good. A couple of nitty-gritty items: what telemetry will you share for p95 computation (raw histograms or pre-aggregated)?
[13:18] Priya Shah: Raw traces and histograms; we deliver both CSV and dashboards.
[13:24] Liam Chen: Any known model variants you recommend for payments - accuracy vs latency?
[13:30] Priya Shah: For short auth templates, smaller quantized 7B variants are often sufficient; for nuanced chat, 13B or ensembles might be better. We'll run quality regressions on your prompt set too.
[13:44] Ethan Ruiz: One more - do you have any guidance for warm-up strategies before peak windows?
[13:50] Priya Shah: Warm-up ramps and pre-warming sessions are recommended; for Dedicated you can keep keep-alive workers to avoid cold starts. We'll include warm-up scripts.
[14:02] Jared Kim: OK let's do a quick recap and next steps.
[14:06] Priya Shah: Recap: 1) Customer to share prompt set and traffic profile by 2026-07-02. 2) Redwood to run hosted + dedicated benches (7B q4 and 13B q4 variants) including auth burst, chat sustained, streaming first-byte metrics. 3) Send security pack and pricing. 4) Schedule joint bench week of 2026-07-06.
[14:30] Maya Ortiz: Thanks everyone. We'll send the sample prompts today and pair with Priya for the bench details.
[14:36] Jared Kim: Thanks - we'll follow up with the bench plan and calendar invite.
[14:42] (meeting ends)

Notes: Transcript contains some transcription noise and occasional speaker labeling ambiguity (e.g., short interruptions). Bench plan to include: defined ramp profiles, sequence length buckets, streaming first-byte checks, per-GPU tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 latencies, and raw traces for customer analysis.
